messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Farmer
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 76

**Patient Vignette: Mr. T.**

Mr. T. is a 42-year-old farmer of South Eastern Asian descent, married with three children. He presents with a calm, weathered demeanor, his hands calloused and stained from years of working the rice paddies. He speaks in a measured, deliberate manner, often pausing to look at the floor before answering a question. He came to therapy at the persistent urging of his wife, who is “worried I am not the same man.”

The trauma began three years ago, when his youngest son, then four years old, was diagnosed with a severe bacterial infection that led to septic shock. Mr. T. describes the day as “normal” until his son, usually running and laughing, became limp and unresponsive. He remembers the frantic drive to the district hospital, the fluorescent lights of the emergency room, and the doctor’s face as he said, “We need to act fast.” He stayed by his son’s side for seventeen days. He did not sleep. He did not eat. He prayed to his ancestors and made bargains with God. He remembers the exact sound of the heart monitor’s alarm, the way the IV tubes looked like thin, clear snakes, and the smell of antiseptic that still makes his stomach turn.

His son survived. He is now a healthy, active seven-year-old. But for Mr. T., the ordeal never ended.

He now works the land with a vigilance that borders on obsession. Every morning, before the sun rises, he checks his son’s breathing, pressing a hand to his small chest until he feels the steady rise and fall. He has installed a thermometer in every room of the house. He takes his son’s temperature three times a day, logging it in a notebook. When the boy has a common cold, Mr. T. cannot function. He becomes rigid, his jaw tight, his eyes scanning for signs of the same bluish tint he saw in the hospital. He drives his son to the clinic for any cough, any sniffle, despite the doctor assuring him it is nothing.

At work, in the fields, he cannot focus. The repetitive motion of planting rice, which once brought him a sense of peace, now feels hollow. He is constantly startled by the sound of a bird taking flight or a tractor backfiring. He has stopped driving the family’s truck because the memory of that frantic ride to the hospital is triggered by the feel of the steering wheel. His wife now handles all errands that require the road.

He avoids his son’s school functions, terrified that a call will come, that he will have to run to the hospital again. He avoids the pediatric wing of the hospital entirely, taking a different route to the market even if it adds twenty minutes. He has stopped visiting his own aging parents, who live near the hospital, because the proximity is too much.

At night, the dreams come. Not of the illness itself, but of the waiting. He dreams of a white room, the sound of a single beeping machine, and a voice that says, “We need to act fast.” He wakes in a cold sweat, his heart pounding, and checks on his son. He does this two, sometimes three times a night. His wife has started sleeping in the other room.

He feels a profound, unshakable guilt. He believes he should have recognized the symptoms sooner, that he should have driven faster, that his prayers were not enough. He feels he has failed as a father. He describes himself as “a shell of a man,” going through the motions of farming, of fatherhood, of marriage, but feeling nothing real. He cannot remember the last time he laughed with his children. He feels disconnected from his community, unable to share his burden because “they would think I am weak.”

Mr. T. is a man who survived his son’s illness, but who has not yet survived the memory of it. He lives in a perpetual state of high alert, a farmer who no longer feels safe on his own land, a father who cannot trust his own child’s health. He is exhausted, hollow, and haunted by a past that refuses to stay buried.
